A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ASUKA and provide readable text, equations, figures and tables supporting comparison. v2 has no separate appendix; v3 includes three supplementary pages. Additional FLUX results referenced but absent from v3 are not treated as available evidence.

before.justification: v2 reports original Places2 and MISATO experiments, component ablations, qualitative results and a user study in Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–9.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and reports additional FLUX, face-dataset, text-guided inpainting and ablation results, including supplementary Tables 5–9.

M1.justification: v3 extends the existing pipeline to ControlNet-based FLUX and generalizes latent augmentation to a rectified-flow coefficient schedule. The MAE prior, linear/self-attention alignment, prior-substitution strategy and decoder augmentation remain intact; this is a backend adaptation rather than a replacement of the core method.

E1.justification: Places2 and the four MISATO domains are retained. v3 adds face inpainting on CelebA-HQ and FFHQ and a separate text-guided decoder evaluation using images from text-to-image-2M, substantially extending domain and task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds SD-IP, SD-T2I, SD-CAEv2 and SD-LaMa comparisons. Tables 2 and 5 additionally evaluate FLUX and BLIP2-caption-guided SD. SD-token matches v2's SD-prompt in description and original scores; SD-Repaint remains in quantitative comparisons despite disappearing from the shortened qualitative grid.

E3.justification: v3 introduces CLIP@mask and Gradient@edge alongside the four retained metrics, and uses CLIPScore in a new decoder evaluation on 1,000 randomly sampled text-guided images. FLUX and alternative conditioning configurations add experimental settings. The stated SD training budget and masking recipe remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds prior-substitution schedule sensitivity tests in Table 6 and separate MAE-only/decoder-only controls in Table 9. It also investigates alternative prior-conditioning mechanisms and BLIP2 caption guidance. The original MAE, alignment and decoder ablations, user study and self-attention failure case are retained, partly in the supplement.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The user study retains 40 images, 100 valid questionnaires and the same preference percentages; its relocation and terminology changes do not alter statistical reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds results for new comparators, metrics, FLUX, face datasets and supplementary experiments. In Table 1, ASUKA's MISATO FID/U-IDS/P-IDS change from 11.460/0.368/0.256 to 11.495/0.423/0.312; its original Places2 scores remain unchanged. Decoder and alignment ablation scores also change. Supplementary Table 10 retains the old full-model values without explaining the discrepancy, so these revisions cannot be attributed confidently to a performance improvement.

T1.justification: Equation (1) extends the diffusion-only formulation to coefficients a and b, distinguishing a²+b²=1 for diffusion from a+b=1 for rectified flow. The diffusion case remains equivalent, but the flow constraint extends the mathematical specification. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden ASUKA from an SD-specific improvement to a framework for diffusion and rectified-flow inpainting models. v3 additionally claims plug-and-play decoder applicability to text-guided inpainting and presents two targeted evaluation metrics as contributions. The original two-component contribution remains.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking pixel-space models' edge-gradient results to latent-compression color shifts and attributing weaker BLIP2 guidance to captions describing the whole image rather than the masked region. It also explains the retraining consequences of changing the VAE encoder. The existing latent-gap explanation and self-attention limitation are retained.

D1.justification: Supplementary Sections 6 and 8 identify the ControlNet-based FLUX backbone, describe its conditioning and specify fine-tuning from its original decoder using the stated SD decoder setup. Most existing implementation information—including learning rates, batch sizes, augmentation strengths and the prior schedule—is preserved and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands related work with image harmonization and object insertion/removal discussions, distinguishing its problem from compositing inconsistencies and conventional inpainting-model development. It also positions ASUKA relative to rectified-flow models and additional conditioning methods such as IP-Adapter, T2I-Adapter and CAE v2.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, with terminology shifting toward unwanted object insertion and color consistency. Method subsections are reorganized, the standalone dataset section is redistributed, and implementation details, the user study, MAE ablation and limitations move into supplementary sections.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout and extensively reorganizes displays. It removes v2 Figure 1, shortens the main qualitative grid, combines or separates existing figure panels, expands and color-ranks Table 1, and splits v2's composite Table 2 across main-text and supplementary tables. Several additional result tables are introduced.

improvement.justification: The new component and prior-schedule controls, alternative-conditioning comparisons and broader evaluations strengthen evidence for ASUKA's design choices and applicability. These gains are limited by unexplained score discrepancies between v3 Tables 1 and 10, unclear CLIP@mask scaling, and absent FLUX results promised in the appendix. The added controlled comparisons support a modest overall improvement, while these reporting problems limit confidence in the expanded claims.
